# Wattle — full reference for agents

Generated by scripts/build.mjs. Sections: AGENTS.md, brand book, tokens.css, then every component's props and guide.


---

# Instructions for AI coding agents

This repository is **Wattle**, a design system. There are two kinds of work here:

- **Building an app with Wattle**: read "Building an app with Wattle" below.
- **Changing Wattle itself**: read "Changing Wattle" and the git rules further down.

## Building an app with Wattle

### Read these first, in this order

1. `README.md`: the brand book. It covers voice, colour rules, type, space, motion and component guidance. Its rules are requirements, not suggestions.
2. `components.json`: every component, with its group, a one-line summary, its props (TypeScript) and the path to its guide.
3. `components/<Name>/README.md`: the guide for each component you use. It says what you provide, what the component does, and the do's and don'ts.
4. `examples/starter.html`: a complete working app. Copy its structure.

`llms-full.txt` holds all of the above in one file, if you'd rather read a single document.

### Loading Wattle

Wattle is plain files with no package to install:

```html
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://bharathwaaj.github.io/wattle/tokens.css">
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://bharathwaaj.github.io/wattle/components/bundle.css">
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/react@18.3.1/umd/react.production.min.js"></script>
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/react-dom@18.3.1/umd/react-dom.production.min.js"></script>
<script src="https://bharathwaaj.github.io/wattle/components/bundle.js"></script>
```

Every component is on `window.Wattle` (`const { Button, Card } = window.Wattle`). Set `data-theme="light"` or `"dark"` on `<html>`.

**In a React or Vite project:** copy `tokens.css`, `components/bundle.css` and `components/bundle.js` into the app (for example, under `src/wattle/`). Then load them in this order:

```js
import React from 'react';
import ReactDOM from 'react-dom';
window.React = React; window.ReactDOM = ReactDOM;   // the bundle reads these globals
import './wattle/tokens.css';
import './wattle/bundle.css';
await import('./wattle/bundle.js');                 // defines window.Wattle
export const { Button, Card, ActionButton /* … */ } = window.Wattle;
```

Types are in `components/index.d.ts`.

### Rules every app must follow

- **Use Wattle components before writing your own.** Check `components.json` first. Cards are built from parts like DateBlock, MetaList, Stat, Progress, Avatar and Badge. Don't hand-style those.
- **Use tokens for every colour, space, radius and shadow**: `var(--ink)`, `var(--space-4)`, `var(--radius-md)`. Never hard-code hex values or pixel spacing that a token covers.
- **One wattle-yellow action per screen.** It's the primary Button or ActionButton. Yellow is never text on a light background, never a border, and never an icon colour.
- **Checked or on states use `ink`**, not yellow. That covers Checkbox, Radio, Switch and Tag.
- **Borders, not shadows.** Cards use a hairline border. Shadows are only for things that float: Dialog, DropdownMenu, Tooltip and Toast.
- **Say it in words.** Status, counts and errors need text, not just colour: "3 seats left", "Selected", "Overdue".
- **Write the way the brand book says**: sentence case, buttons that start with a verb, short sentences.
- **Motion confirms a result.** Use ActionButton for commitments (Book → Booked), UndoButton or HoldButton for deletes, and `Wattle.toast()` for things confirmed elsewhere. Don't add animation that the components don't already have.
- **Accessibility**: give every icon-only button an `aria-label`, give every input a visible label, and keep the focus ring.
- **If Wattle has no component for something**, build it in the app from tokens. Follow the nearest component's look, and say in your summary that it isn't part of Wattle yet.

### Icons

Pass Lucide names to `icon` props, or use `<Icon name="…" />`. `components.json` → `icons` lists the available names. Don't use other icon sets.

## Changing Wattle

- The sources are `tokens.json`, `README.md`, `components/` (`bundle.js`, `bundle.css`, `index.d.ts`, plus a `README.md` and `preview.html` per component) and `assets/`.
- **After any change, run `node scripts/build.mjs`.** It regenerates `tokens.css`, `components.json`, `llms.txt` and `llms-full.txt`, so apps and agents stay in sync. Commit the generated files together with the change.
- A new component needs four things: its code in `components/bundle.js` (added to the `@ds-bundle` header list and to `window.Wattle`), styles in `bundle.css`, types in `index.d.ts`, and a `components/<Name>/` folder with `README.md` and `preview.html`. Line 1 of `preview.html` is `<!-- @dsCard group="…" height=N subtitle="…" -->`. The docs site picks it up automatically.
- `bundle.js` is one classic script with no imports. It must never contain the literal text `</script` or `<!--`.
- `index.html` is the GitHub Pages docs site. `design-system.json` is the index for the Claude design-system artifact: these files are mirrored there under `project/`.

## Git commit messages

- Include a concise subject and a human-readable body in every commit message.
- Follow Conventional Commits: type(scope): description. Omit the scope
  when it adds no useful context. Common types include feat, fix, docs,
  style, refactor, test, build, ci, perf, and chore.
- Use an imperative description (for example, "add" rather than "added"),
  with no trailing period. Aim for a subject of 50 characters or fewer;
  do not exceed 72, including the type and scope.
- Make the subject summarize the entire change. Include critical release
  or time-sensitive context when relevant.
- Refer to documentation sections by their titles, not section numbers.
- Separate the subject from the body with a blank line.
- Explain what changed and why in the body, including relevant impact or
  motivation. Attribution trailers alone do not count as a body.
- Start with the problem or missing behavior and who it affected, then
  explain the change and why it addresses that problem. Omit low-level
  implementation details unless they are not apparent from the diff.
- Include relevant verification results and limitations when useful.
  Only claim checks that actually ran; state what was not verified.
- Add useful context rather than repeating the subject or filling space.
  Summarize related changes instead of listing every minor edit.
- Use hyphen bullets for all body details, not prose paragraphs. Wrap body
  lines at 72 characters and indent continuation lines.
- Use plain text without Markdown emphasis, backticks, or code fences.
  Keep attribution and other Git trailers unbulleted in a separate footer.
- Base the message on the actual diff. Describe important dependency,
  binary asset, or encoding changes specifically rather than vaguely.
- Inspect opaque or binary changes with appropriate tools before
  describing them; do not infer their contents from filenames alone.
- For submodule updates, summarize the actual upstream changes rather
  than reporting only a pointer or commit hash.
- Reference relevant issues in the footer. Use closing references only
  when the commit fully resolves the issue; never invent issue IDs.
- Identify breaking changes with a BREAKING CHANGE: footer describing
  the impact and required migration.
- For reverts, use revert: followed by the original subject, and include
  a body bullet stating "This reverts commit <full SHA>." Explain why.
- When amending, review the existing commit and staged changes. Write the
  message for the final combined commit, not just the amendment.
- Only create or amend commits when the user explicitly asks.

## Change and pull request hygiene

- Keep each commit a single, coherent, stable change, and keep pull
  requests focused on one feature or behavior rather than unrelated work.
- Review your own diff before handing it off. Remove accidental changes,
  unused code, and unrelated files.
- Explain what a pull request changes, why it is needed, and how it was
  verified. Mention important trade-offs or rejected alternatives.
- Propose significant architecture, schema, API, or tooling changes
  before implementing them. Include deployment or migration plans when
  relevant.
- Avoid unnecessary rebases during review, since rewriting history can
  make review comments and incremental changes harder to follow.

## Code reviews

- Prioritize bugs, security, compatibility, performance, and tests that
  verify the intended behavior. Check whether the stated goals are met.
- Give specific, actionable, respectful feedback. Distinguish blocking
  correctness issues from optional suggestions and stylistic nitpicks.
- Prefer clear simplifications over clever rewrites. Reduce risk and
  unnecessary complexity rather than pursuing perfection.
- Use automated checks for enforceable style rules instead of spending
  review effort on formatting.


---

# Brand book


**Warm earth, one sharp yellow.** Wattle is a design system based on the Yellow-wattled Lapwing (*Vanellus malabaricus*), a ground bird of dry fields in India. Its colours are mostly sandy brown and taupe, with one bright yellow patch on its face.

This system does the same thing: calm, earthy neutrals almost everywhere, with yellow kept for the one thing that matters on each screen.

## Content fundamentals

- **Plain and warm.** Write the way you'd explain something to a colleague. Use short sentences and everyday words.
- **One idea at a time.** Keep paragraphs to 1–3 sentences. Use headings and bullets to make pages easy to scan.
- **Sentence case** for every title, button and label: "Create course", not "Create Course".
- **Verbs on buttons.** "Save changes", "Add student". Avoid "OK" and "Submit".
- **Tags and overlines** use the `label` style in uppercase, and nothing else does.

## Visual foundations

### Colour

The palette comes from the bird's plumage.

| Token | Comes from | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ink` | Cap black | Text and icons |
| `wattle` | Face wattle and eye ring | The one accent: primary action, selection, highlight |
| `earth` | Upperparts brown | Large fills, illustration, first chart series |
| `taupe` | Neck and breast | Quiet fills, tags, second chart series |
| `surface-100` | Pale underparts | Page background |
| `wing` | Wing-tip brown | Deep bands, footers, tooltips |

**Rules**

- **One yellow per view.** `wattle` marks the primary action or the current selection. If two things are yellow, neither one stands out.
- **Wattle is a fill, not a line.** On light surfaces it reaches only 1.4:1 contrast, so never use it for text, thin borders or focus rings. Text on wattle is always `on-wattle`. In the dark theme, wattle *can* be used as text (11.8:1).
- **Neutrals carry the page.** Use `surface-100`, `surface-200`, `ink` and `ink-muted` for most of the interface. Keep `earth` and `taupe` for fills and illustration. Use `earth` as text only at 24px and above.
- **Borders, not shadows.** Separate raised `surface-200` from the page with a `hairline` border. Controls use `border-strong` (3:1 or better).
- **Shadows only for things that float.** Use `shadow-overlay` for dropdowns, popovers, tooltips and toasts, and `shadow-dialog` for modals and sheets. Use both together with `surface-200` and a `hairline` border. Never put a shadow on a card or an input.
- **Focus rings** are 2px `ink` with a 2px offset.
- **`danger`** is only for errors and destructive actions. Keep it small.

### Themes

- **Light**: the bird by day, with cream ground and black ink.
- **Dark**: the field at dusk, with a near-black warm ground and cream ink. Wattle, earth, taupe and wing look the same in both themes.

### Type

- **Newsreader** (display): a calm, slightly condensed editorial serif for `display`, `heading-1` and `heading-2`. It has optical sizes, so large headings tighten up and small ones stay open, and long titles fit on fewer lines.
- **Manrope** (sans): a clean, friendly sans for all UI and body text.
- Both are free on Google Fonts. Load them with weights 400–700.

### Space and shape

- **Spacing** follows `space-1` (4px), `space-2` (8px), `space-4` (16px), `space-6` (24px) and `space-10` (40px). Cards use `space-4` padding, the gap between cards is `space-6`, and sections are separated by `space-10`.
- **Radius**: `radius-sm` for inputs and tags, `radius-md` for cards, and `radius-pill` for buttons and chips. The pill shape echoes the round eye ring.

## Components

Components are React 18 components, published as `window.Wattle` from `components/bundle.js`. Load the stylesheet first (`components/bundle.css`, which also loads both fonts).

- **Button**: the primary variant is the wattle action, one per view. Use secondary, ghost and danger for everything else.
- **Input**: always give it a visible label. Errors show as text, not just colour.
- **Card**: a `surface-200` panel with a hairline border. One frame, many patterns, from events and deadlines to media, metrics and empty states. The Card guide lists them.
- **Badge**: a small pill for status or category, in neutral, strong or danger. Never wattle.
- **Status, CountBadge, Tag**: a dot and a word for state, a number pill for counts, and chips for filters and choices.
- **Forms**: Checkbox, RadioGroup, Switch, Select and Textarea share Input's label, hint and error. Checked controls, Switch included, fill `ink`, which keeps `wattle` for actions.
- **Navigation**: Tabs, with an `ink` underline that grows in under the active tab.
- **Overlays**: Dialog (native `<dialog>`, `shadow-dialog`), Toaster and `Wattle.toast()`, Tooltip and DropdownMenu (`shadow-overlay`). These are the only places shadows appear.
- **Building blocks**: IconDisc, DateBlock, MetaList, Progress, Checklist, Avatar, Stat, Sparkline and SeatMap. These are the parts the card patterns are made from, so reuse them and don't restyle by hand.
- **Icon**: draws any of the starter icons inline in `currentColor`. Button, Input and Card accept an `icon` prop that takes an icon name, like `icon="search"`.

### Motion

Buttons move only to confirm that something happened or to prevent a mistake.

- **ActionButton**: the button becomes its own result, like Book → Booked, Add to calendar → Added, or Copy link → Copied.
- **ProgressButton**: a fill sweeps across while slow work runs. It ends on success, or on an error with a retry.
- **HoldButton**: press and hold to delete, as the danger outline draws itself around the button.
- **UndoButton**: deletes at once, with 5 seconds to undo.
- **ReactionButton**: star, like and save toggles that pop and burst on.
- **Button `effect`**: `nudge` and `sweep` hover hints.

Keep motion between 150 and 500ms, and announce every result to screen readers. Everything goes still when the OS setting "reduce motion" is on.

Every focus state is the same: a 2px `ink` ring with a 2px offset.

## Iconography

Icons come from **Lucide** (v0.460.0, ISC licence). They're adjusted to a 1.5px stroke and sit on a 24px grid. The starter set is in the Icons asset group.

- Draw icons in `ink` or `ink-muted`, using `danger` only for error states. Never colour an icon `wattle`.
- Size an icon to the text next to it: 24px by default, 20px in dense UI.
- Outline icons only, with no filled or multi-colour icons. The full rules are in the Icons group README.

## Logo

The mark is the lapwing's **eye ring**: a `wattle` ring and dot on a cap-black disc. The wordmark is "Wattle" in Newsreader 600, converted to outlines.

- On light backgrounds, use `wattle-lockup.svg` or `wattle-mark.svg`. On dark backgrounds, use the `-dark` versions.
- Use the mark alone where space is tight, such as favicons, avatars and app icons.
- Never put the yellow ring on a light background without its disc. Never recolour or stretch the mark.

## Origin of the palette

The colours are a refined blend of two hand-estimated palettes taken from photographs of the Yellow-wattled Lapwing. One was an illustrative palette card. The other was based on a Cornell Lab *Birds of the World* photograph. Neither palette was pixel-sampled, so the yellow was adjusted (`#ECD43E`) to sit between the vivid wattle and the softer tone seen in natural light. No photographs are included in this system.

# tokens.css

```css
/* Wattle — generated from tokens.json by scripts/build.mjs. Do not edit by hand. */
:root, [data-theme="light"] {
  --surface-100: #F7F4EC;
  --surface-200: #FFFDF8;
  --ink: #1F1D1B;
  --ink-muted: #5E5447;
  --hairline: #D6CEBE;
  --border-strong: #8F8373;
  --wattle: #ECD43E;
  --on-wattle: #1F1D1B;
  --earth: #85715A;
  --taupe: #A69A8B;
  --wing: #43392F;
  --danger: #B3361F;
  --shadow-overlay: 0 1px 2px rgba(67, 57, 47, 0.10), 0 8px 24px rgba(67, 57, 47, 0.14);
  --shadow-dialog: 0 2px 6px rgba(67, 57, 47, 0.12), 0 24px 56px rgba(67, 57, 47, 0.22);
}
[data-theme="dark"] {
  --surface-100: #1A1816;
  --surface-200: #24211E;
  --ink: #F3EFE6;
  --ink-muted: #B8AD9C;
  --hairline: #3D3730;
  --border-strong: #7A6F60;
  --wattle: #ECD43E;
  --on-wattle: #1F1D1B;
  --earth: #85715A;
  --taupe: #A69A8B;
  --wing: #43392F;
  --danger: #F08A6E;
  --shadow-overlay: 0 1px 2px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.40), 0 8px 24px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.50);
  --shadow-dialog: 0 2px 6px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.45), 0 24px 56px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.60);
}
:root {
  --space-1: 4px;
  --space-2: 8px;
  --space-4: 16px;
  --space-6: 24px;
  --space-10: 40px;
  --radius-sm: 6px;
  --radius-md: 14px;
  --radius-pill: 999px;
  --font-display: "Newsreader", Georgia, "Times New Roman", serif;
  --font-sans: "Manrope", system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", sans-serif;
}
.display { font-family: var(--font-display); font-size: 56px; line-height: 60px; font-weight: 600; letter-spacing: -0.02em; }
.heading-1 { font-family: var(--font-display); font-size: 36px; line-height: 42px; font-weight: 600; letter-spacing: -0.01em; }
.heading-2 { font-family: var(--font-display); font-size: 24px; line-height: 30px; font-weight: 600; }
.body { font-family: var(--font-sans); font-size: 16px; line-height: 24px; font-weight: 400; }
.body-sm { font-family: var(--font-sans); font-size: 14px; line-height: 20px; font-weight: 400; }
.label { font-family: var(--font-sans); font-size: 12px; line-height: 16px; font-weight: 700; letter-spacing: 0.06em; }
.caption { font-family: var(--font-sans); font-size: 13px; line-height: 18px; font-weight: 500; }
```

# Button (Actions)

```ts
export interface ButtonProps extends React.ButtonHTMLAttributes<HTMLButtonElement> {
  /** primary: the one wattle action per view. secondary (default): everything else. ghost: low-emphasis, toolbars. danger: destructive. */
  variant?: 'primary' | 'secondary' | 'ghost' | 'danger';
  /** md is 40px tall (default), sm is 32px. */
  size?: 'md' | 'sm';
  /** Hover/focus effect: nudge slides the trailing icon, sweep fills with ink from the left. */
  effect?: 'nudge' | 'sweep';
  /** Icon before the label: a Lucide name or a React node. With no children it makes an icon-only button; pass aria-label. */
  icon?: IconName | React.ReactNode;
  /** Icon after the label, e.g. 'arrow-right'. */
  iconEnd?: IconName | React.ReactNode;
}
```

Triggers an action. Pill-shaped, 40px tall (32px with `size="sm"`).

## Variants

- **primary**: wattle fill with `on-wattle` text. Use it for the one main action on a view, and use only one per view.
- **secondary** (default): `surface-200` with a `border-strong` outline. Use it for every other action.
- **ghost**: no fill. Use it for Cancel, toolbars and low-emphasis actions next to a primary.
- **danger**: `danger` outline and text. Use it for destructive actions, and confirm them first.

## You provide

- `children`: the label. Start with a verb and use sentence case, e.g. "Create course".
- `onClick`, and any other native button attribute. `type` defaults to `button`.
- `variant` and `size`, optionally.
- `icon`: an optional icon before the label, given as a Lucide name (`"plus"`) or a React node. Its size follows the button: 18px, or 16px for `sm`.
- `iconEnd`: an optional icon after the label. Use it for direction, like `"arrow-right"` or `"chevron-down"`.
- **Icon-only**: pass `icon` with no children, and always pass `aria-label`. The button then becomes a 40px circle (32px for `sm`).

## Hover effects

Set `effect` for a small hint on hover and keyboard focus:

- **`nudge`**: the trailing icon slides out and back in. Use it with `iconEnd: "arrow-right"` for buttons that move you forward.
- **`sweep`**: `ink` fills the button from the left, and the text turns to `surface-200`. Use it on secondary buttons that lead somewhere bigger, like "View all courses".

Both turn off when the OS setting "reduce motion" is on.

## Do and don't

- Do put the primary button last in a row of actions.
- Don't use two primary buttons on one view. If two things look equally important, one of them isn't.
- Don't put an icon-only primary button where a label fits.
- Use one icon per button at most, and only where it helps people scan, like add, download or delete. Don't add icons just to decorate.
- Focus shows a 2px `ink` ring with a 2px offset, so never remove the outline.


---

# ActionButton (Motion)

```ts
export interface ActionButtonProps {
  label: React.ReactNode; icon?: IconName | React.ReactNode;
  doneLabel: React.ReactNode; doneIcon?: IconName | React.ReactNode;
  /** morph (default): shrink to spinner and grow back; flip: icon turns over; swap: in-place swap. */
  animation?: 'morph' | 'flip' | 'swap';
  variant?: 'primary' | 'secondary' | 'ghost'; doneVariant?: 'primary' | 'secondary' | 'ghost';
  size?: 'md' | 'sm';
  /** The work; return a Promise. Rejecting returns the button to idle. */
  onAction?: (e: React.MouseEvent) => unknown;
  /** Return to idle after this many ms (e.g. Copy link). */
  resetAfter?: number; loadingLabel?: string; className?: string;
  /** Latch: clicking the done state returns to idle and calls onUndo. */
  undoable?: boolean; onUndo?: (e: React.MouseEvent) => void; undoHint?: string;
}
```

A button that shows its own result. Click "Book" and it changes to "Booked" in place, with no toast or page change.

## Animations

- **morph** (default): the label slides away, and the button shrinks to a circle with a spinner. It then grows back as the done state with a check that pops in. Use it for commitments like Book, Enrol or Join.
- **flip**: the icon turns over like a page into the done icon. Use it for small saves like "Add to calendar" → "Added".
- **swap**: the icon and label swap in place. Use it with `resetAfter` for repeatable actions like "Copy link" → "Copied".

## You provide

- `label`, `icon`: the idle state.
- `doneLabel`, `doneIcon`: the result, such as "Booked" with a check (the default icon).
- `onAction`: the work to do. Return a Promise, and the button waits for it. If it rejects, the button goes back to idle.
- `variant`: `primary` by default. `doneVariant` defaults to secondary when the variant is primary, because a finished action is no longer the main call to action.
- `resetAfter`: optional. The number of ms to wait before going back to idle.
- `undoable`: optional. It makes the button **latch**: clicking "Booked" again goes back to "Book" and calls `onUndo`. The button reports `aria-pressed`, and `undoHint` (a tooltip) says what clicking again does.
- `size`, `className`: optional.

## Behaviour

- A loading state lasts at least 700ms for morph and 250ms otherwise, so the change can be seen.
- The result is announced in a polite live region, so screen readers hear "Booked".
- When the OS setting "reduce motion" is on, states change instantly and the spinner slows down.
- Once done, the button is `aria-disabled` unless `resetAfter` or `undoable` is set.

## Do and don't

- Use morph for one main action per screen. It's the yellow moment.
- Don't use ActionButton for destructive actions. Use HoldButton or UndoButton instead.


---

# ProgressButton (Motion)

```ts
export interface ProgressButtonProps {
  label: React.ReactNode; icon?: IconName | React.ReactNode;
  runningLabel?: string; doneLabel?: React.ReactNode; errorLabel?: React.ReactNode;
  /** Call setProgress(0-100) as work goes; resolve or reject when finished. */
  onAction?: (setProgress: (p: number) => void) => Promise<unknown>;
  variant?: 'primary' | 'secondary' | 'ghost'; size?: 'md' | 'sm'; className?: string;
}
```

A button for slower work, like a submission or an upload. A darker fill sweeps across it as the work runs, with the percentage in the label. It ends on a success or an error.

## You provide

- `label`, `icon`: the idle state, e.g. "Submit worksheet".
- `runningLabel`: shown with the percentage, e.g. "Submitting 44%".
- `doneLabel`, `errorLabel`: the end states. An error turns the button `danger` and shakes it once. Clicking it again retries.
- `onAction(setProgress)`: call `setProgress(0–100)` as the work goes, and return a Promise that resolves or rejects.
- `variant`: `secondary` by default.

## Do and don't

- Do use it when the work takes more than about a second and you can report progress.
- Do write error labels that say what to do next: "Upload failed, try again".
- Don't fake progress you can't measure. Use ActionButton's spinner instead.


---

# HoldButton (Motion)

```ts
export interface HoldButtonProps {
  label?: React.ReactNode; doneLabel?: React.ReactNode;
  /** Hold time in ms, default 1000. */
  duration?: number; onConfirm?: () => void; size?: 'md' | 'sm'; hintId?: string; className?: string;
}
```

A destructive action that needs a press and hold instead of a confirmation dialog. A `danger` outline draws itself around the pill while it's held. Let go early and nothing happens. Hold for the full time and the trash lid pops, the label changes to "Deleted", and the button fades.

## You provide

- `label`: say "hold" in it, e.g. "Hold to delete".
- `doneLabel`: e.g. "Deleted".
- `duration`: optional, in ms. The default is 1000.
- `onConfirm`: runs when the hold completes.
- `size`: optional.

## Behaviour

- It works with a mouse, touch, or keyboard. On a keyboard, hold Enter or Space.
- The outline fills linearly over `duration`. Letting go rewinds it in 200ms.
- "Deleted" is announced to screen readers.

## Do and don't

- Do use it for permanent deletes where an undo isn't possible.
- Don't use it for anything that can be undone. UndoButton is faster for people.


---

# UndoButton (Motion)

```ts
export interface UndoButtonProps {
  label?: React.ReactNode; doneLabel?: React.ReactNode; undoLabel?: React.ReactNode;
  /** Undo window in ms, default 5000. */
  duration?: number;
  onDelete?: () => void; onUndo?: () => void; onCommit?: () => void;
  size?: 'md' | 'sm'; className?: string;
}
```

Deletes at once, then gives people a few seconds to change their mind. The button turns into "Deleted · Undo", with a line shrinking along the bottom. If the line runs out, the delete is final.

## You provide

- `label`: e.g. "Delete lesson".
- `doneLabel`: e.g. "Lesson deleted".
- `undoLabel`: optional. The default is "Undo".
- `duration`: optional, in ms. The default is 5000.
- `onDelete`: runs on click. Hide the item straight away.
- `onUndo`: runs if Undo is pressed. Restore the item.
- `onCommit`: runs when the time is up. Delete for real.

## Behaviour

- Focus moves to Undo when the delete happens, so keyboard users can undo with one key press.
- "Lesson deleted. Undo available." is announced to screen readers.

## Do and don't

- Do prefer this over a confirmation dialog whenever the delete can be held back for a few seconds.
- Don't shorten the time below 4 seconds.


---

# ReactionButton (Motion)

```ts
export interface ReactionButtonProps {
  kind?: 'star' | 'heart' | 'bookmark';
  /** Accessible name; the count is appended. */
  label: string;
  count?: number; defaultPressed?: boolean; onChange?: (pressed: boolean) => void; className?: string;
}
```

A toggle for small, personal reactions: star, like or save. Turning it on pops the icon and bursts a ring of dots. Turning it off is quiet.

## Kinds

- **star**: fills `wattle` with an `ink` outline, and bursts `wattle` and `earth` dots.
- **heart**: fills `danger` and bursts `danger` and `taupe` dots. Use it with a `count`.
- **bookmark**: fills `ink`, and the ribbon drops in from above. It has no burst.

## You provide

- `kind`: `"star"`, `"heart"` or `"bookmark"`.
- `label`: the accessible name, like "Star", "Like" or "Save". The count is added to it automatically.
- `count`: optional. It shows a number that rolls up or down as the toggle changes.
- `defaultPressed`, `onChange(pressed)`: optional.

## Behaviour

- It uses `aria-pressed`, so screen readers say "Star, toggle button, pressed".
- When "reduce motion" is on, there's no pop or burst. The fill still changes.

## Do and don't

- Do keep reactions small and next to the thing they're about.
- Don't use them for real commitments like booking or paying. Use ActionButton for those.
- The star is the one place where wattle shows as an icon fill. It always keeps its `ink` outline, so it reads on light backgrounds.


---

# Input (Forms)

```ts
export interface InputProps extends React.InputHTMLAttributes<HTMLInputElement> {
  /** Visible label, always provide one. */
  label?: React.ReactNode;
  /** Helper text under the field, in ink-muted. */
  hint?: React.ReactNode;
  /** Error message; sets aria-invalid and a danger border. */
  error?: React.ReactNode;
  /** Decorative icon at the start of the field, e.g. 'search'. */
  icon?: IconName | React.ReactNode;
  /** Decorative icon at the end of the field, e.g. 'calendar'. */
  iconEnd?: IconName | React.ReactNode;
}
```

A single-line text field with a visible label, an optional hint and an optional error message.

## You provide

- `label`: always provide one. Placeholders are examples, not labels.
- `hint`: optional helper text in `ink-muted`.
- `error`: an optional message. It turns the border `danger`, sets `aria-invalid` and is linked to the input for screen readers.
- `icon`: an optional icon at the start of the field, like `"search"` or `"filter"`. It's drawn in `ink-muted` and is decorative only.
- `iconEnd`: an optional icon at the end of the field, like `"calendar"` or `"chevron-down"`.
- Any native input attribute (`type`, `value`, `onChange`, `placeholder`, `disabled`…). The component handles `id` if you don't pass one.

## Do and don't

- Do write errors as a fix: "Use letters and numbers only", not "Invalid input".
- Do keep the error text, because colour alone doesn't mark the error. The component adds a warning icon in front of it.
- Don't rely on an icon to explain the field. The label must still say what goes in it.
- Don't put a wattle border or fill on fields. Yellow is for actions and selection, not focus.
- Focus shows a 2px `ink` ring and an `ink` border.


---

# Checkbox (Forms)

```ts
export interface CheckboxProps extends React.InputHTMLAttributes<HTMLInputElement> { label: React.ReactNode; hint?: React.ReactNode; indeterminate?: boolean; }
```

A single on/off choice with a visible label. It's a native checkbox underneath, styled with an `ink` fill when checked.

## You provide

- `label`, and optionally `hint`.
- `checked` and `onChange`, or `defaultChecked`. Any native input attribute also works.
- `indeterminate`: for a "select all" box when only some items are chosen. It shows a dash.

## Do and don't

- Do use it for choices that take effect when a form is submitted. For settings that apply at once, use Switch.
- Do write labels as positive statements: "Email me a weekly summary", not "Don't email me".


---

# RadioGroup (Forms)

```ts
export interface RadioGroupProps { legend: React.ReactNode; options: { value: string; label: React.ReactNode; hint?: React.ReactNode; disabled?: boolean }[]; value?: string; defaultValue?: string; onChange?: (value: string) => void; name?: string; hint?: React.ReactNode; inline?: boolean; className?: string; }
```

One choice from a short list, in a fieldset with a legend. The chosen option shows an `ink` ring and dot. Arrow keys move between options, as with native radios.

## You provide

- `legend`: the question, e.g. "Batch timing".
- `options`: an array of `{ value, label, hint?, disabled? }`.
- `value` and `onChange(value)`, or `defaultValue`.
- `hint`: optional, for the whole group. `inline`: lays two or three short options out in a row.

## Do and don't

- Use it for 2–5 options. For more, use Select.
- Always pre-select the most common option, unless choosing is the point.


---

# Switch (Forms)

```ts
export interface SwitchProps { label: React.ReactNode; hint?: React.ReactNode; checked?: boolean; defaultChecked?: boolean; onChange?: (on: boolean) => void; disabled?: boolean; id?: string; className?: string; }
```

An on/off setting that applies straight away. When it's on, the track fills `ink` and the `surface-200` knob slides across with a check. This matches how Checkbox and Radio show "on", and keeps `wattle` for actions. It uses `role="switch"` and `aria-checked`.

## You provide

- `label`, and optionally `hint`.
- `checked` and `onChange(on)`, or `defaultChecked`.
- `disabled`: optional.

## Do and don't

- Use it only when the change happens at once, with no Save button. Inside a form, use Checkbox.
- Label the setting, not the action: "Class reminders", not "Turn on reminders".


---

# Select (Forms)

```ts
export interface SelectProps extends React.SelectHTMLAttributes<HTMLSelectElement> { label?: React.ReactNode; hint?: React.ReactNode; error?: React.ReactNode; options: (string | { value: string; label: React.ReactNode })[]; placeholder?: string; }
```

A native dropdown, styled to match Input: a `border-strong` outline, a chevron, and the same label, hint and error. Because it's native, keyboards, screen readers and phone pickers all work as expected.

## You provide

- `label`, `hint`, `error`.
- `options`: strings, or `{ value, label }` objects.
- `placeholder`: an unselectable first line, like "Choose a class".
- `value` and `onChange`, or `defaultValue`.

## Do and don't

- Use it for 6 or more options, or where space is tight. For fewer, RadioGroup shows every option at once.
- Sort options in the order people expect, like numbers ascending or alphabetical.


---

# Textarea (Forms)

```ts
export interface TextareaProps extends React.TextareaHTMLAttributes<HTMLTextAreaElement> { label?: React.ReactNode; hint?: React.ReactNode; error?: React.ReactNode; }
```

Multi-line text, styled like Input. It starts 96px tall, and people can drag it taller.

## You provide

- `label`, `hint`, `error`, `placeholder`, `rows`.
- `maxLength`: optional. It shows a "120 / 280" count, which turns `danger` and is announced once the text passes 90% of the limit.
- `value` and `onChange`, or `defaultValue`.

## Do and don't

- Do set `maxLength` when there's a real limit, and say why in the hint if it's tight.
- Use a placeholder as a prompt, not as instructions. Instructions go in the hint.


---

# Tabs (Navigation)

```ts
export interface TabsProps { tabs: { id: string; label: React.ReactNode; content: React.ReactNode; icon?: IconName | React.ReactNode; count?: number }[]; label?: string; defaultTab?: string; onChange?: (id: string) => void; className?: string; }
```

Switches between views of the same thing, like a course's lessons, tests and notes. The active tab is `ink` with a 2px `ink` underline that grows in. The others are `ink-muted`.

## You provide

- `tabs`: an array of `{ id, label, content, icon?, count? }`. A `count` shows a small pill after the label.
- `label`: names the tab list for screen readers.
- `defaultTab` and `onChange(id)`: optional.

## Behaviour

- It follows the WAI-ARIA tabs pattern. Arrow Left and Right move and select, Home and End jump to the ends, and only the active tab sits in the Tab order.

## Do and don't

- Keep labels to one or two words. Use 2–6 tabs.
- Don't use tabs for steps in a process. People expect to move between tabs freely.


---

# Dialog (Overlays)

```ts
export interface DialogProps { open: boolean; onClose?: () => void; title: React.ReactNode; children?: React.ReactNode; footer?: React.ReactNode; dismissable?: boolean; className?: string; }
```

A modal that asks one question or holds one short task. It's built on the native `<dialog>`, so focus stays inside, Esc closes it, and the page behind becomes inert. It uses `surface-200`, a hairline, `radius-md` and `shadow-dialog` over a dimmed backdrop.

## You provide

- `open` and `onClose`.
- `title`: a question or a task, like "Leave Batch A?".
- `children`: one or two sentences about what happens next.
- `footer`: the actions, with the safe choice first and the committing one last.
- `dismissable`: set it to `false` to stop a backdrop click from closing it.

## Do and don't

- Do say the consequence in the body: what's lost, what stays.
- Prefer UndoButton or HoldButton for deletes. Use a dialog when the action needs explaining.
- Don't stack dialogs or put forms longer than 3 fields in one.


---

# Toaster (Overlays)

Short messages that confirm something happened elsewhere on the page. They rise in at the bottom centre on an `ink` pill (cream in the dark theme) with `shadow-overlay`, then leave on their own.

## Use

1. Put `<Toaster />` once, near the root of the app.
2. Call `Wattle.toast(message, options)` from anywhere.

## Options

- `tone`: `neutral` (default), `success` (adds a check) or `danger` (adds a warning icon).
- `actionLabel` and `onAction`: one action, like Undo or Retry.
- `duration`: the default is 4 seconds, or 6 seconds when there's an action.

## Behaviour

- Toasts are announced in a polite live region. At most 3 show at once, and the oldest leaves first.

## Do and don't

- Do keep messages short and in the past tense: "Changes saved".
- Don't use a toast for errors that block the work. Show those inline, next to the problem.
- Don't toast something the button already shows. ActionButton's "Booked" needs no toast.


---

# Tooltip (Overlays)

```ts
export interface TooltipProps { label: React.ReactNode; children: React.ReactElement; side?: 'top' | 'bottom'; delay?: number; }
```

A short `ink` label that appears on hover or keyboard focus, after 250ms. It names what an icon-only control does. Esc hides it.

## You provide

- `label`: two or three words.
- `children`: exactly one focusable element, usually an icon-only Button. It gets `aria-describedby`.
- `side`: `top` (default) or `bottom`. `delay`: optional, in ms.

## Do and don't

- Use it to name icon-only buttons. The button still needs its own `aria-label`.
- Never put information only in a tooltip. Touch screens can't hover.
- Don't put links or buttons inside a tooltip.


---

# DropdownMenu (Overlays)

```ts
export interface DropdownMenuProps { items: DropdownMenuItem[]; label?: React.ReactNode; ariaLabel?: string; icon?: IconName | React.ReactNode; variant?: 'primary' | 'secondary' | 'ghost'; size?: 'md' | 'sm'; align?: 'start' | 'end'; }
```

A button that opens a short list of actions, such as an item's "…" overflow menu or "Sort by". The menu sits on `surface-200` with a hairline and `shadow-overlay`.

## You provide

- `items`: an array of `{ label, icon?, onSelect, danger?, disabled?, shortcut? }`, or `{ divider: true }`.
- `label`: a text trigger like "Sort by" with a chevron. Leave it out for an icon-only "…" trigger, and pass `ariaLabel` instead (the default is "More actions").
- `variant` (default `ghost`), `size`, `icon`, `align: "end"` (opens to the left).

## Behaviour

- It follows the WAI-ARIA menu button pattern. Opening it focuses the first item. Arrow Up and Down, Home and End move between items. Esc closes it and returns focus to the trigger. Tab or a click outside also closes it.

## Do and don't

- Keep it to 7 items at most. Put destructive actions last, after a divider, in `danger`.
- Don't hide the main action in a menu. If people use it often, make it a button.


---

# Card (Layout)

```ts
export interface CardProps extends React.HTMLAttributes<HTMLElement> {
  /** Element to render, default section. */
  as?: keyof JSX.IntrinsicElements;
  /** Link target when as="a" (shortcut cards). */
  href?: string;
  /** Small uppercase overline above the title. */
  eyebrow?: React.ReactNode;
  /** Card title, set in Newsreader. */
  title?: React.ReactNode;
  /** Actions row under a hairline, usually Buttons. */
  footer?: React.ReactNode;
  /** Full-bleed image or illustration across the top of the card. */
  media?: React.ReactNode;
  /** empty: dashed border on a transparent ground, centred; for empty states. */
  variant?: 'default' | 'empty';
  /** Set false to drop the hairline above the footer and separate it with space instead. */
  divider?: boolean;
  /** Ink border for a chosen card in a selectable list. */
  selected?: boolean;
  /** Icon shown in a 40px circle above the eyebrow. */
  icon?: IconName | React.ReactNode;
}
```

A raised `surface-200` panel with a `hairline` border and `radius-md` corners. Each card holds one thing: an event, a booking, a person, a result.

## Patterns

Card is one frame. What changes from card to card is what goes inside it. The preview shows eleven patterns, and each one answers a different question. Every piece inside is a Wattle component, so build them from these parts and not from one-off CSS.

| Pattern | Answers | Built from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Announcement** | What do I need to know? | `IconDisc` (strong), a bold line, a sentence, a timestamp and an icon-only dismiss `Button`. Use it full width. |
| **Event** | When and where? | `DateBlock` and `MetaList` (time, host), with an `ActionButton` (flip): "Add to calendar" → "Added to calendar". |
| **Booking** | Can I join, and when? | `Badge`s in the eyebrow, a one-line pitch, a `MetaList` (day, time, places left), then Book (`ActionButton`, morph, `undoable`) and Details (ghost). Booking lowers the places-left count, and clicking Booked again cancels it. |
| **Media** | What does it look like? | The `media` prop: a full-bleed image or illustration across the top, then the title. Read, plus a bookmark `ReactionButton`. |
| **Availability** | How much is left? | `Stat` ("4 seats left") and `SeatMap`, with Reserve a seat (`ActionButton`, morph, `undoable`). The count drops and your seat pops in. |
| **Progress** | How far along am I? | `Progress`, "12 of 24", and a secondary `Button` with `effect="nudge"`, using `divider={false}`. |
| **Metric** | How are we doing? | `Stat` with a trend in words, and a `Sparkline`. |
| **Checklist** | What's left to do? | `Checklist`, with a count in the eyebrow that updates. |
| **Person** | Who is this? | `Avatar`, the name, a `Status` ("Teaching now"), and a row of `Badge`s, using `divider={false}`. |
| **Link** | Where can I see more? | `as="a"`: a title, one sentence, then an `ink` "Open …" line with an arrow, set `space-4` below the text so it doesn't read as part of the sentence. The whole card is the link. |
| **Empty state** | What do I do first? | `variant="empty"`: a dashed border, an icon, one sentence, and one action. |

Clickable cards come in two kinds:

- **Shortcut card**: use `as="a"` with an `href`. The whole card is the link, so put no buttons inside it.
- **Choice card**: use `as="button"` with `role="radio"`, `aria-checked` and `selected`, inside a wrapper with `role="radiogroup"`. Say "Selected" in the eyebrow as well.

## You provide

- `title`: set in Newsreader at heading-2 size.
- `eyebrow`: an optional uppercase overline in `ink-muted`, e.g. "Course". It can hold an icon, like the check on a selected choice card.
- `icon`: an optional icon in a 40px circle above the eyebrow, given as a Lucide name or a React node. Use it for shortcut cards.
- `children`: the body text, in `ink-muted`.
- `media`: an optional image or illustration, shown full-bleed across the top. Give images real alt text.
- `variant`: `"empty"` for empty states, with a dashed border, a transparent ground and centred content.
- `footer`: optional actions, usually Buttons, under a hairline. The footer is pushed to the bottom, so footers line up across a row.
- `divider`: set it to `false` to drop the footer's hairline and separate the footer with space instead. Use this when the card is short, or when its content already ends cleanly, like a progress bar or a badge row. A card with fewer lines reads calmer.
- `selected`: optional. It gives the card an `ink` border.
- `as`: the element to render, `section` by default. Cards rendered as `a` or `button` get a hover border and the standard focus ring.

## Do and don't

- Do size each card to its content. In a dashboard, stack cards in columns rather than stretching them to match a row, because stretched cards end up with empty space inside.
- Don't start a footer with a ghost button. Its padding makes the label look indented, so use a secondary button.
- Do mark the selected choice in words too ("Selected" in the eyebrow), not just with the border.
- Don't put buttons inside a shortcut card. The card itself is the link.
- Use motion buttons where an action changes the card: Book, Reserve, Add to calendar, Save. Let the card react as well, by updating the count or filling the seat, so the result shows in the content and not only on the button.
- Keep to one primary (wattle) button across a whole screen of cards. Every other card action is secondary or ghost.
- Don't add shadows. Wattle uses borders, not shadows.
- Don't fill cards with wattle or add a coloured left border.
- Don't nest cards inside cards.


---

# Badge (Status)

```ts
export interface BadgeProps extends React.HTMLAttributes<HTMLSpanElement> {
  /** neutral (default) for categories, strong for the one important thing, danger for problems. */
  tone?: 'neutral' | 'strong' | 'danger';
  /** Optional 12px icon before the text. */
  icon?: IconName | React.ReactNode;
}
```

A small pill label for status or category, like "New", "Beginner" or "Batch A". It is not clickable.

## Tones

- **neutral** (default): `surface-100` with a `hairline` border and `ink` text. Use it for categories and tags.
- **strong**: an `ink` fill with `surface-200` text, which inverts in the dark theme. Use it for the one thing that's new or important on a card.
- **danger**: a `danger` outline and text. Use it for problems like "Overdue" or "Failed".

## You provide

- `children`: one or two words, in sentence case.
- `tone`: optional.
- `icon`: an optional 12px icon before the text, as a Lucide name.

## Do and don't

- Do put badges in a Card's `eyebrow`, or in a row under a person or item.
- Use one strong badge per card at most.
- Don't make badges wattle. Yellow is for actions and selection.
- Don't use a badge as a button or filter chip.


---

# CountBadge (Status)

```ts
export interface CountBadgeProps { count: number; max?: number; label?: string; showZero?: boolean; className?: string; }
```

A small `ink` pill with a number, like unread messages or new submissions. The number rolls when it changes, and anything over `max` shows as "99+".

## You provide

- `count`. It hides itself at 0 unless you pass `showZero`.
- `label`: what's being counted, e.g. "unread". Screen readers hear "3 unread".
- `max`: the default is 99.

## Do and don't

- Put it right after the thing it counts.
- Don't use it for status words. Use Badge or Status for those.


---

# Status (Status)

```ts
export interface StatusProps { tone?: 'neutral' | 'live' | 'active' | 'done' | 'danger'; children: React.ReactNode; className?: string; }
```

A coloured dot and a word that say what state something is in. It's lighter than a Badge, so use it in lists and tables.

## Tones

- **live**: a `danger` dot that pulses. Use it only for things happening right now, like a live class.
- **active**: a `wattle` dot with an `ink` ring. Use it for "in progress".
- **done**: an `ink` dot.
- **neutral** (default): a `border-strong` dot. Use it for draft or scheduled items.
- **danger**: a `danger` dot and text. Use it for overdue or failed items.

## Do and don't

- The word always carries the meaning, and the dot only helps people scan.
- Don't use more than one `live` status per screen.


---

# Tag (Status)

```ts
export interface TagProps { children: React.ReactNode; onRemove?: () => void; selected?: boolean; onClick?: () => void; label?: string; className?: string; }
```

A chip for things people choose and can take away again, like subjects, batches and filters.

## Two kinds

- **Removable**: pass `onRemove`, and the chip gets an × button named "Remove Physics".
- **Toggle**: pass `selected` and `onClick`. When it's on, it fills `ink` with a check, and it uses `aria-pressed`.

## You provide

- `children`: one or two words.
- `label`: optional. The name used in "Remove …" when the children aren't plain text.

## Do and don't

- Use toggles for filters and removable tags for choices already made.
- Don't use Tag for status. Badge and Status are for that.


---

# IconDisc (Building blocks)

```ts
export interface IconDiscProps { icon: IconName | React.ReactNode; tone?: 'neutral' | 'strong' | 'danger'; size?: number; label?: string; className?: string; }
```

A single icon in a round disc. It anchors an announcement, an empty state or a shortcut card.

## You provide

- `icon`: a Lucide name.
- `tone`: `neutral` (default) has a `surface-100` fill with a hairline border. `strong` is `wing` with a cream icon, for announcements. `danger` is an outline, for warnings.
- `size`: in px. The default is 40, and the icon is drawn at half that size.
- `label`: only when the disc stands alone and means something. Otherwise it's hidden from screen readers.

## Do and don't

- Use one disc per card at most.
- Don't use a disc as a button. If it needs to be clickable, use an icon-only Button.


---

# DateBlock (Building blocks)

```ts
export interface DateBlockProps { date?: string | number | Date; month?: string; day?: number | string; label?: string; className?: string; }
```

A calendar-page date: the month in small caps above the day in large Newsreader. Put it beside an event's title.

## You provide

- Either `date` (anything `new Date()` accepts), or `month` and `day`.
- `label`: optional. The full spoken date, e.g. "Tuesday 18 November". It defaults to "18 NOV".

## Do and don't

- Pair it with a MetaList for the time and place.
- Don't use it for ranges or deadlines. Write those out in words.


---

# MetaList (Building blocks)

```ts
export interface MetaListProps { items: { icon?: IconName | React.ReactNode; text: React.ReactNode }[]; className?: string; }
```

Rows of small details (dates, times, places, people), each with a 16px icon, in `ink-muted`.

## You provide

- `items`: an array of `{ icon, text }`, where `text` can be any node.

## Do and don't

- Keep it to 2–4 rows, with one fact per row.
- Use icons people know: calendar for the day, clock for the time, user for people.


---

# Progress (Building blocks)

```ts
export interface ProgressProps { value: number; max?: number; label: string; showValue?: boolean; className?: string; }
```

A thin `earth` bar that shows how far along something is. It animates when the value changes.

## You provide

- `value`, and `max` (default 100).
- `label`: required for screen readers, e.g. "Course progress".
- `showValue`: optional. Adds the percentage after the bar.

## Do and don't

- Do write the progress in words nearby too, like "12 of 24 lessons".
- Don't use it for tasks that are still running. Use ProgressButton or a spinner.


---

# Checklist (Building blocks)

```ts
export interface ChecklistProps { items: { label: React.ReactNode; done?: boolean }[]; done?: boolean[]; onChange?: (done: boolean[]) => void; label?: string; className?: string; }
```

A short list of tick boxes. They're real checkboxes under the styling, so keyboards and screen readers work as usual. Done items are struck through in `ink-muted`.

## You provide

- `items`: an array of `{ label, done }`.
- `done` and `onChange(doneArray)` to control it, or leave both out to let it keep its own state.
- `label`: names the list for screen readers.

## Do and don't

- Do show a count nearby, like "3 of 5 done".
- Keep it to 3–7 items. Anything longer is a task list, not a checklist.


---

# Avatar (Building blocks)

```ts
export interface AvatarProps { name: string; initials?: string; size?: number; className?: string; }
```

A round initials badge for a person: `ink` on `taupe` (6:1), in Newsreader.

## You provide

- `name`: used for the initials (first and last word) and as the accessible name.
- `initials`: optional, to override the computed ones.
- `size`: in px. The default is 48.

## Do and don't

- Do put the name in text next to it. The avatar supports the name, it doesn't replace it.
- Don't colour avatars by person. Taupe keeps lists calm.


---

# Stat (Building blocks)

```ts
export interface StatProps { value: React.ReactNode; unit?: React.ReactNode; label?: React.ReactNode; trend?: React.ReactNode; trendDirection?: 'up' | 'down' | 'flat'; className?: string; }
```

One big number in Newsreader, with an optional unit and a one-line trend. The number rolls in when it changes.

## You provide

- `value`, `unit` (optional) and `label` (optional overline).
- `trend`: written out in words, e.g. "Up 4 points on last week".
- `trendDirection`: `up` (default), `down` or `flat`. It sets the arrow, and the words carry the meaning.

## Do and don't

- Show one stat per card, or a row of 2–4 in a dashboard.
- Don't colour trends red or green. Say what happened in the words.


---

# Sparkline (Building blocks)

```ts
export interface SparklineProps { data: number[]; height?: number; label?: string; className?: string; }
```

A small `earth` line chart with an `ink` dot on the latest value. It shows the shape, not exact values.

## You provide

- `data`: an array of numbers, oldest first. It needs at least 2.
- `height`: optional. The default is 56.
- `label`: describes the trend for screen readers, e.g. "Average score over 8 weeks, from 62 to 86".

## Do and don't

- Pair it with a Stat that gives the current number.
- Don't add axes or gridlines. If people need the values, use a proper chart.


---

# SeatMap (Building blocks)

```ts
export interface SeatMapProps { total: number; taken: number; columns?: number; mine?: boolean; label?: string; className?: string; }
```

A grid of dots that shows how many places are taken and how many are left. Taken places are filled `earth`, free ones are `border-strong` rings, and the person's own place pops in `wattle` with an `ink` ring.

## You provide

- `total`, `taken`, and `columns` (default 10).
- `mine`: makes the last taken place the person's own.
- `label`: optional. It defaults to "36 of 40 places taken, 4 left".

## Do and don't

- Do say the number in words too, like "4 seats left".
- Keep the total under about 60. For more, use a Progress bar.


---

# Icon (Media)

```ts
export interface IconProps extends React.SVGAttributes<SVGSVGElement> {
  /** Which icon to draw. */
  name: IconName;
  /** Size in px, default 24. */
  size?: number;
  /** Accessible name; only for icons that stand alone. Without it the icon is aria-hidden. */
  label?: string;
}
```

Draws one of the 31 starter icons inline as SVG. Icons come from Lucide v0.460.0 (ISC licence) and are drawn with a 1.5px stroke in `currentColor`.

## You provide

- `name`: the icon's name, such as `"search"` or `"trash-2"`. `Wattle.Icon.names` lists every name.
- `size`: optional, in px. The default is 24.
- `label`: give a label only when the icon stands alone and carries meaning. Without one, the icon is hidden from screen readers.
- Colour comes from the parent's CSS `color`. Use `ink` or `ink-muted`, and `danger` only for errors.

## Do and don't

- Do use the `icon` props on Button, Input and Card instead of placing an Icon inside them yourself.
- Don't colour icons `wattle`.
- Don't mix in icons from other sets. For a new icon, take it from Lucide v0.460.0, add it to the bundle, and add its file to the Icons asset group.
